speaker: Emma Grede
title: The Truth Behind Building Skims ft Emma Grede
question: When launching a challenger retail brand into a mature apparel category, how does studying the market-leading incumbent actually shape positioning?
guest: In the beginning, we were like, "Wow, there is this incumbent." Whenever I'm starting a business, I always take aim at something—at the competition—and I am one of those people that will learn everything about that business. I probably know the Levi's pricing structure more than I know my own. I know when they're in the sale, I know what's happening on the site, I know when a new thing's launched, because you have to become obsessed with what you do. You need to go in and learn from the best. For me, Levi's still today is the absolute pinnacle in that space. So we were looking at that business to say, who is the most successful, best-in-class version, and how can we differentiate and do something that's right for our customer for a new idea of what being a woman is all about? It's taking the best from who's doing it at the top, and finding your own way to truly differentiate and bring something fresh.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Studying the incumbent matters less for what to copy than for revealing what the leader cannot easily do. A market leader's position is built on commitments: a broad audience, a price architecture, wholesale relationships, a brand meaning it has spent decades reinforcing. Each strength carries a trade-off, and those trade-offs are where a challenger finds room.

In practice, the analysis does three things. First, it defines the category's reference point, since customers will judge you against the leader whether you like it or not; your positioning becomes "unlike X, we…". Second, it exposes underserved segments and frustrations: fit ranges ignored, occasions neglected, customers who feel the leader's brand is no longer "for them". Third, it identifies moves the incumbent would find costly to match, because responding would alienate its core customer or cannibalise its margins.

Under Armour against Nike (performance fabric, underdog grit) and Lululemon against generic athletic wear (a premium, community-led women's focus) both followed this pattern.

The caution: defining yourself purely as the anti-leader is fragile. The contrast gets attention, but the positioning must rest on a benefit customers value independently.

models.answer:
Studying a market-leading incumbent is less about finding features to copy and more about mapping the structural compromises forced by their scale. In a mature apparel category, the leader sets consumer expectations around baseline price, fit, and convenience, establishing the category conventions a challenger must understand before choosing where to break them. Because incumbents depend on mass volume, broad demographic appeal, and often legacy wholesale channels, they inevitably underserve specific body types, specialized use cases, or shifting cultural tastes.

Analyzing the leader’s negative reviews, sizing complaints, assortment bloat, and promotional habits reveals exactly where mass-market averaging creates customer friction. Effective challenger positioning exploits these rigidities, turning the incumbent’s size into a liability in spaces where it cannot easily respond without cannibalizing margins, alienating retail partners, or diluting its core brand. Rather than claiming to be vaguely better, the challenger anchors against the leader’s defaults to claim a sharp wedge—such as precision fit, technical materials, or a distinct subcultural aesthetic—giving overlooked shoppers an immediate, unmistakable reason to switch.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Studying the leader mostly shows a challenger where it shouldn't compete and which flank to attack. Mature apparel categories tend to be organised around the incumbent's way of doing things: its price structure, fit standards, distribution and brand story set what shoppers expect. A careful teardown of its assortment, margins, store experience, customer reviews and marketing shows which strengths are too costly to copy, such as scale-driven pricing, broad distribution or heritage. It also shows the compromises the leader has to make to serve a mass base. Those compromises are the openings: customers it underserves, such as extended sizes or particular body types, categories it treats as an afterthought, or a sustainability claim its supply chain can't back up. Warby Parker against Luxottica, Allbirds against athletic giants and Everlane's "radical transparency" against opaque markups all made the leader's weakness their own reason to exist. The incumbent also acts as a reference point. Shoppers judge the challenger against it, so positioning works best when it is clearly different on one or two dimensions that matter and stays familiar on everything else. The main risk is ending up as a cheaper copy, a position scale economics usually punishes.

Studying the market leader helps a challenger decide where to meet customer expectations and where to give shoppers a reason to switch. The incumbent’s assortment, pricing, fit, and messaging show what shoppers are used to. Reviews and customer interviews can reveal which of those expectations matter most and where shoppers still make compromises.

For example, if the leading denim brand offers a wide range of washes but shoppers consistently struggle to find jeans that fit both their waist and hips, a challenger could build its positioning around that fit problem. It would still need to deliver the quality and price shoppers expect, then make the difference tangible through its cuts, fit guides, and try-on experience. The opening is strongest when a specific group of shoppers cares enough to switch and the challenger can deliver on the promise consistently.
